title: Psychological and physiological effect in humans of touching plant foliage - using the semantic differential method and cerebral activity as indicators
research_question: This study examines the psychological and physiological effects of touching plant foliage by using an evaluation profile of the subjects' impressions and investigating cerebral blood flow.

participants.description: 14 young Japanese men aged from 21 to 27 years (mean ± standard deviation: 23.6 ± 2.4).
participants.recruitment: Subjects gave informed consent to the experiment in accordance with the protocol reviewed and approved by the Human Investigation Committee of Chiba University.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four different tactile samples: a plate of aluminum (metal), a piece of velveteen (fabric), a leaf of natural pothos (Epipremnum aureum), and a leaf of artificial pothos made of resin. Each material was held between two 10cm x 10cm square papers with a 5cm square window cut out.

measures.instrument: Semantic differential (SD) method with ten pairs of adjectives (warm/cold, smooth/rough, soft/hard, natural/artificial, familiar/unfamiliar, kind/unkind, calming/stimulating, peaceful/anxious, pleasant/unpleasant, like/dislike)
Near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS; NIRO-300; Hamamatsu Photonics, JAPAN) measuring oxygenated hemoglobin in two channel sensors on the right and left sides of the forehead (prefrontal areas).

findings.mechanism: Fabric was significantly warmer than metal, natural pothos, and artificial pothos.
Fabric was significantly rougher than metal.
Fabric was significantly softer than metal and artificial pothos.
Fabric was significantly more natural than metal.
Fabric was significantly more 'kind' than metal, natural pothos, and artificial pothos.
Fabric was significantly more 'calming' than metal, natural pothos, and artificial pothos.
Fabric was significantly more 'peaceful' than metal, natural pothos, and artificial pothos.
Fabric was significantly more 'pleasant' than metal, natural pothos, and artificial pothos.
Fabric was significantly more 'liked' than metal, natural pothos, and artificial pothos.
Metal was significantly colder than artificial pothos, and fabric and natural pothos.
Metal was significantly smoother than fabric, natural pothos, and artificial pothos.
Metal was significantly harder than fabric, natural pothos, and artificial pothos.
Metal was significantly more artificial than fabric, natural pothos, and artificial pothos.
Artificial pothos was significantly harder than fabric.

findings.antecedent: Touching natural pothos vs. artificial pothos
findings.mechanism: No remarkable differences between the stimuli of natural and artificial pothos psychologically.
findings.quote: No difference between artificial and natural pothos was seen in any of the adjectival descriptors.

findings.consequent: Cerebral blood flow (oxygenated hemoglobin) in both frontal areas
findings.mechanism: Metal stimulus caused a stress response in human cerebral blood flow, likely due to the cold stimulus and high thermal conductivity of aluminum.
findings.quote: the CBF of both frontal areas for the metal sample increase compared with the pre-stimulus results from 10 s to 20 s.

findings.consequent: Cerebral blood flow (oxygenated hemoglobin) in both prefrontal areas
findings.mechanism: Fabric stimulus induced physiological calm, consistent with pleasant and kind psychological impressions.
findings.quote: significant decreases of both pre-frontal areas are continuously seen from 15 s to 75 s for the fabric sample.

findings.consequent: Cerebral blood flow (oxygenated hemoglobin) in left prefrontal area
findings.mechanism: Natural pothos stimulus caused a slight, significant reduction in CBF, implying an unconscious physiological calming reaction ('low road' affect) despite neutral psychological evaluation.
findings.quote: the natural pothos sample showed significant decreases in the left prefrontal area around 70 s

findings.consequent: Cerebral blood flow (oxygenated hemoglobin) in right prefrontal area
findings.mechanism: Natural pothos stimulus caused a slight, significant reduction in CBF, implying an unconscious physiological calming reaction ('low road' affect) despite neutral psychological evaluation.
findings.quote: and in the right prefrontal area around 30 s.

findings.mechanism: No significant difference in CBF for artificial pothos stimulus.
findings.quote: However, there was no significant difference in the stimulus of artificial pothos.

mechanisms: The affective reaction caused by tactile stimuli can occur through 'low road' (unconscious physiological effects) or 'high road' (conscious subjective experiences) pathways, as proposed by LeDoux.
Physiological stress responses can be induced by cold stimuli, related to the thermal conductivity of materials.

Touching natural plants can induce physiological calmness from an unconscious state, suggesting an essential message from the primitive brain that plants are indispensable to human well-being (triune brain hypothesis).
implementation_implications: Plants, nature, and natural materials bring feelings of relaxation to people.
Touching living plants can cause an unconscious calming response.

tables.description: Pairs of adjectives used in the semantic differential method for evaluating tactile samples.
Summary of Steel-Dwass's test results comparing subjective SD method scores for metal, fabric, natural pothos, and artificial pothos.

limitations: The results might have been different if leaves with various different surface types had been used.
It is difficult to specify exactly what activity is taking place in the prefrontal area due to the limitations of NIRS, which has only two points of measurement.
